title: Case basics and the core scenarios

questions.q: Which combination of skills are case interviewers mainly trying to observe?
opts: Detailed prior knowledge of the client's industry
Speed at reaching a final answer, even without showing the logic
Structured thinking, comfort with numbers, and clear communication under ambiguity
Ability to recall as many named business frameworks as possible
questions.ex: Cases are designed to show how you break down an unfamiliar problem, handle the math, and explain your thinking; industry expertise is not expected.

questions.q: A candidate gets every calculation right but jumps between ideas without ever stating a structure. What is the interviewer most likely to mark down?
opts: Organization and communication of the approach
Quantitative ability
Business intuition about the industry
Enthusiasm for consulting
questions.ex: The math was correct, so the gap is in laying out a clear structure and walking the interviewer through it.

questions.q: Which is the strongest way to answer "Tell me about yourself" in a consulting interview?
opts: A chronological walk through every role on your resume
A short list of personal hobbies so the interviewer gets to know the real you
A detailed explanation of the case frameworks you have studied
A one-to-two minute story linking your background, a few chosen highlights, and why consulting is the logical next step
questions.ex: A concise, curated narrative that ends with why you want this job shows judgment and communication skill, which is what the question tests.

questions.q: Which answer to "Why consulting?" is most convincing?
opts: The chance to travel and work with smart people
Specific reasons tied to your own experiences, such as a project where solving a structured business problem energized you
Consulting pays well and keeps your future options open
You have read a lot about the firm and admire its brand
questions.ex: Interviewers look for genuine, specific motivation backed by evidence from your past; generic perks sound rehearsed and apply to anyone.

questions.q: The interviewer has just read you the case prompt. What should you do first?
opts: Present a full framework immediately to show confidence
Briefly restate the problem and confirm the client's objective
Ask for all available data on costs and revenue
Give your recommendation based on your first instinct
questions.ex: Summarizing the prompt and confirming the goal makes sure you are solving the right problem before you structure anything.

questions.q: Which sequence best reflects a disciplined approach to a case?
opts: Structure, listen, hypothesize, clarify, then summarize
Listen, hypothesize, summarize, then clarify
Clarify, summarize, listen, then structure
Listen, clarify, structure, form a hypothesis, then summarize
questions.ex: You need the facts (listen, clarify) before building a structure, then test a hypothesis and close with a summary.

questions.q: Estimate annual toothbrush sales in a country of 50 million people, assuming 90% of people use a toothbrush and each user replaces it 3 times a year.
opts: 135 million toothbrushes
150 million toothbrushes
45 million toothbrushes
1.35 billion toothbrushes
questions.ex: 50 million x 0.9 = 45 million users, and 45 million x 3 replacements = 135 million toothbrushes per year.

questions.q: A city has 1,000,000 households. 40% own a dog, and each dog-owning household spends $50 per month on dog food. What is the annual dog food market in the city?
opts: $20 million
$200 million
$240 million
$480 million
questions.ex: 1,000,000 x 40% = 400,000 households; 400,000 x $50 = $20 million per month; x 12 months = $240 million per year.

questions.q: A client's profits have fallen for two years while revenue has stayed flat. Where should you focus first?
opts: Price, since raising prices is the fastest fix
Sales volume by customer segment
Competitor market share trends
Costs, split into fixed and variable, to find which ones have grown
questions.ex: Profit = revenue - costs; with revenue flat, the decline must come from rising costs, so break costs down to locate the increase.

questions.q: A product sells for $50, has a variable cost of $30 per unit, and the business has fixed costs of $600,000. How many units must it sell to break even?
opts: 30,000 units
12,000 units
20,000 units
7,500 units
questions.ex: Contribution per unit is $50 - $30 = $20, so breakeven = $600,000 / $20 = 30,000 units.

questions.q: A frozen-food maker asks whether it should start selling in a new country. Which structure fits best?
opts: Revenue and cost breakdown of the client's current business only
Target valuation, synergies, and integration risks
Market attractiveness, competitive landscape, client capabilities, entry mode, and expected economics
Cost-based, competitor-based, and value-based pricing
questions.ex: A market-entry question needs to test whether the market is attractive, whether the client can win, how to enter, and whether it pays off.

questions.q: A client has a strong product but no distribution in a new country and needs to be selling there within 12 months. Which entry mode is usually best?
opts: Build its own distribution network from scratch
Acquire or partner with a local company that already has distribution
Enter with prices well below local competitors to force retailers to stock it
Wait until local demand is proven by competitors
questions.ex: Buying or partnering gives immediate access to channels and local know-how, which matters most when speed is the constraint.

questions.q: A target company will earn a steady $10 million profit per year indefinitely. The client requires an 8% return, and the seller is asking $150 million. What does a simple perpetuity valuation suggest?
opts: The target is worth about $125 million, so the asking price is about $25 million too high
The target is worth about $80 million, so the asking price is about $70 million too high
The target is worth about $150 million, so the price is fair
The target is worth about $187.5 million, so the price is a bargain
questions.ex: Perpetuity value = $10 million / 0.08 = $125 million, which is $25 million below the $150 million asking price.

questions.q: A client says it wants to acquire a competitor. What is the most useful first clarifying question?
opts: How many employees does the target have?
Which investment bank is advising on the deal?
What is the target's logo and brand color?
What is the client trying to achieve with the deal, such as growth, new capabilities, or cost synergies?
questions.ex: The deal rationale determines which parts of the analysis matter most and what a good price looks like.

questions.q: A company has launched a new drug that greatly shortens hospital stays and has no direct competitor. Which pricing approach is most appropriate?
opts: Cost-plus pricing, adding a standard markup to production cost
Value-based pricing, anchored on the savings and benefits to patients and payers
Competitor-based pricing, matching the nearest existing treatment
Penetration pricing set as low as possible to maximize volume
questions.ex: With a unique product and large measurable benefits, the price should capture part of the value created rather than reflect cost or a weak comparison.

questions.q: A competitor's moves push the client to consider cutting price from $100 to $90. Variable cost is $60 per unit and it sells 10,000 units today. Roughly how much must volume grow to keep total contribution the same?
opts: About 10%
About 25%
About 33%
About 50%
questions.ex: Contribution today is $40 x 10,000 = $400,000; at $90 it is $30 per unit, so it needs about 13,333 units, a rise of about 33%.

questions.q: Which growth option generally carries the lowest risk?
opts: Launching new products in new markets
Entering a new country with existing products
Selling more of existing products to existing markets
Acquiring a company in an unrelated industry
questions.ex: Market penetration builds on known customers and known products, so it has the fewest unknowns.

questions.q: A factory runs at 95% utilization and demand is forecast to grow 20%. Before recommending a new plant, what should you check first?
opts: Which architect should design the new plant
Whether the demand growth is durable and whether cheaper options, such as extra shifts or outsourcing, could cover it
How fast competitors are building their own plants
Whether the new plant should be twice the size of the current one
questions.ex: A new plant is a large fixed commitment, so confirm the demand is lasting and rule out lower-cost ways to add capacity first.

questions.q: A new cafe has fixed costs of $24,000 per month. The average ticket is $8 and the variable cost per ticket is $2. If it opens 25 days a month, how many tickets per day does it need to break even?
opts: 120 tickets per day
200 tickets per day
4,000 tickets per day
160 tickets per day
questions.ex: Contribution per ticket is $8 - $2 = $6, so $24,000 / $6 = 4,000 tickets per month, or 4,000 / 25 = 160 per day.

questions.q: A client asks you to cut costs by 10%. What is the best first step?
opts: Break the cost base into its components and compare them over time and against competitors to find the biggest gaps
Cut every department's budget by 10% equally
Start with layoffs, since labor is usually the largest cost
Raise prices to offset the costs instead
questions.ex: Understanding where costs sit and which are out of line lets you target the largest, most fixable items rather than cutting blindly.

questions.q: For a cable TV provider, the rise of streaming services that let viewers drop cable entirely is best classified as which of Porter's Five Forces?
opts: Threat of substitutes
Threat of new entrants
Bargaining power of buyers
Rivalry among existing competitors
questions.ex: Streaming meets the same need in a different way, which makes it a substitute rather than a new cable competitor.

questions.q: A product holds 5% share in a market where the leader holds 30%, and the market is growing 18% per year. Where does it sit in the BCG matrix?
opts: Star
Cash cow
Question mark
Dog
questions.ex: Low relative share (about 0.17x the leader) in a fast-growing market is the question mark quadrant.

questions.q: What is the best way to use a one-page framework cheat sheet during an interview?
opts: Recite the closest framework word for word to show preparation
Use it as a starting point and tailor the structure to the specific facts of the case
Use the same framework for every case to stay consistent
Avoid any structure so the answer sounds original
questions.ex: Interviewers reward structures that fit the problem; a memorized framework is a base to adapt, not a script.

questions.q: Which prompt-to-framework pairing belongs on a good cheat sheet?
opts: "Why are profits down?" - Porter's Five Forces only
"Should we enter Brazil?" - fixed vs variable cost breakdown only
"How should we price our new product?" - BCG matrix
"Should we buy Company X?" - the target's market, its financials, synergies, price, and risks
questions.ex: An acquisition question is answered by judging the target, the fit, and the price; the other pairings use a tool that misses the core question.

questions.q: Which closing summary is strongest?
opts: "First we looked at the market, then competitors, then costs, and after all that we think entering could make sense."

"The client should enter the market. It is growing 12% a year, we can reach breakeven in two years, and a partner gives us distribution. The main risk is a price war, so next we should test price sensitivity."
"There are many factors to consider, and more data is needed before we can say anything."
"The market is growing 12% a year and competitors are fragmented, which is interesting."
questions.ex: It leads with the answer, gives the key supporting reasons, and ends with the main risk and a next step.

questions.q: A candidate closes: "We examined revenue, then costs, then the competition, and found several things, so overall the client might consider closing the plant." What is the main weakness?
opts: It recaps the analysis in order instead of leading with a clear recommendation
It is too short to cover the analysis
It should not mention costs in a summary
It makes a recommendation, which candidates should avoid
questions.ex: A strong summary states the recommendation first, then the reasons; a chronological recap buries the answer and sounds unsure.

questions.q: An exhibit shows revenue by region. North went from $40M to $44M; South went from $60M to $54M. Which statement is correct?
opts: Total revenue fell 10%, driven equally by both regions
Total revenue was flat because the regions' changes offset
Total revenue fell 2%, because the South's 10% decline outweighed the North's 10% growth
Total revenue grew 2% thanks to strong growth in the North
questions.ex: Total went from $100M to $98M, a 2% drop; both regions moved 10%, but the South is larger so its $6M loss beat the North's $4M gain.

questions.q: An exhibit shows Year 1 revenue of $200M with cost of goods sold of $120M, and Year 2 revenue of $250M with cost of goods sold of $160M. What happened?
opts: Gross profit fell, and gross margin fell from 40% to 36%
Gross profit rose by $50M, and gross margin stayed at 40%
Gross profit rose by $10M, and gross margin rose from 36% to 40%
Gross profit rose by $10M, but gross margin fell from 40% to 36%
questions.ex: Gross profit went from $80M to $90M, but as a share of revenue it went from 80/200 = 40% to 90/250 = 36%.

questions.q: In a 25-minute practice case you have spent 15 minutes on one branch of your structure. What is the best move?
opts: Summarize what you found, state what it implies, and move to the next most important branch
Keep digging until that branch is fully exhausted
Start over with a new framework
Skip straight to the final recommendation without mentioning the other branches
questions.ex: Managing time means banking your findings and prioritizing the remaining analysis so you can still reach a well-supported answer.

questions.q: A client has revenue of $500M and costs of $450M. Next year revenue stays flat and costs rise 4%. By what percentage does profit fall?
questions.ex: Costs rise to $468M, so profit drops from $50M to $32M, a fall of $18M / $50M = 36%.
